screens.title: Functions and Visibility
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll learn how to write functions that control behavior, security, and gas use in a Solidity contract. Functions are the executable units that accept inputs, optionally change state, return values, and enforce rules. We will look closely at visibility modifiers — public, private, internal and external — and why choosing the right one prevents accidental access and enforces encapsulation. You'll learn state mutability modifiers, view and pure, which help you signal read-only intent and reduce gas when called off-chain. We'll also show how payable marks a function able to accept Ether and how msg. value reports the amount sent. Finally, you'll meet custom modifiers, a compact pattern to reuse access checks like an onlyOwner guard. A concrete code example in this chapter demonstrates these ideas working together: constructor initialization, a payable deposit, an owner-only withdraw, internal helper functions, and a derived contract that can access internal members. Knowing these tools matters because they reduce bugs, tighten access control, and optimize costs. As you explore, ask yourself whether a function truly needs external exposure or can be internalized for safety.

As you study, reflect on one question: which of your contract functions truly need external visibility and which can be internalized for safety?

screens.title: What is a function in Solidity?
screens.narratorSegment: A function in Solidity is a named, executable block that accepts parameters, optionally changes contract state, and may return values. The function signature—its name plus parameter types and return types—forms the contract's callable A P I. Signatures matter because the Ethereum ABI uses them to encode and decode calls, and because clarity in signature design reduces programmer error. For example, a function declared as returns (uint) signals to callers that they will receive a numeric result; marking it view communicates that the call will not alter state. A well-designed function is small, focused, and documents whether it reads or writes state. Common mistakes include over-exposing helpers as public, which expands attack surface, and neglecting to declare return types, which can confuse callers and tools. A concrete example: a function calculateSum(uint a, uint b) declared pure returns (uint) performs only a computation and does not access storage, so it is safe to call off-chain and is gas-free when executed via a read-only provider. Remember: signatures express intent and constraints; use them deliberately to make your contract predictable, testable, and secure. Which of your functions could be simplified to pure or view to clarify intent and reduce costs?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Functions are the contract's API: signature defines inputs and outputs; mutability and visibility define behavior and allowed callers.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › What is a function?
Definition

Function signature and intent

A signature includes the name, parameter types, and return types. Use view or pure when possible to show read-only intent.

Concrete example
function calculateSum(uint a, uint b) public pure returns (uint) {
  return a + b;
}
Misconception
All helpers must be public — false. Make helpers private/internal if not part of API.
Pro tip
Mark pure when you only use parameters; mark view when you read state but do not write it.
Why it matters

Explicit signatures improve interoperability, security, and developer experience. They make it clear how external callers and other contracts should interact with your code.

Key Takeaway

Design functions with clear signatures and mark mutability to communicate intent and reduce gas where possible.

screens.title: Visibility modifiers: public vs private vs internal vs external
screens.narratorSegment: Visibility controls who can call a function and is a central part of contract design. Public functions are the most permissive: they can be called from external accounts or other contracts and also from inside the same contract. Because public is the default, explicitly declaring visibility improves readability. Private functions, by contrast, can only be called from within the defining contract; they cannot be accessed by derived contracts or external callers. Use private for helper logic that must never be shared. Internal functions sit between private and public: they are inaccessible externally but can be called by derived contracts. This makes internal suitable for shared logic in an inheritance hierarchy. External functions can only be called from outside the contract. They read arguments from calldata directly, which can be more gas-efficient for large arrays or strings compared to public functions that copy arguments into memory. A typical pattern is to expose an external function as the public A P I that validates inputs and then delegate to an internal function for the shared implementation, reducing duplication and protecting helpers. A common misconception is thinking external can be called internally like a normal function; it cannot. When designing visibility, ask: who should be allowed to call this, and could making it internal or private reduce risk?

keyIdea.title: Visibility summary
keyIdea.text: public: external+internal. private: only this contract. internal: this contract + derived. external: only external callers and contracts; gas-efficient for calldata.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Visibility modifiers
At-a-glance comparison
public
Callable externally and internally. Default when omitted.
private
Only within the same contract; not visible to derived contracts.
internal
Accessible in this contract and derived contracts; not external.
external
Callable only from outside; reads args from calldata for gas savings.
Pattern: external API → internal implementation
function doActionExternal(uint[] calldata data) external {
  _doActionInternal(data);
}

function _doActionInternal(uint[] memory data) internal {
  // shared implementation
}
Example note
Use calldata on external functions to avoid copying large arrays into memory, saving gas when possible.
Common mistake
Trying to call an external function internally as if it were public will fail or be inefficient; prefer internal delegation.

screens.title: Private and Internal: encapsulation and inheritance
screens.narratorSegment: Private and internal control how logic is shared across inheritance boundaries. Private restricts access strictly to the same contract body. Use it for helper functions or operations that must never be visible to children—for example, a low-level decrement helper that should only be used internally to avoid misuse. Internal, however, opens the function to derived contracts, enabling reuse inside an inheritance hierarchy without exposing it to external callers. This is often the right choice when you want to let child contracts extend behavior or read shared state variables like _sharedData in our example contract. A common pattern is to implement core behavior in internal functions and leave thin public or external wrappers for validation or input parsing. Misconceptions to avoid: internal is not public; it still cannot be called from external accounts. Another subtle point: state variables marked internal are accessible in derived contracts, but private variables are not. When designing inheritance, decide if children should have controlled access to your internals or if stricter privacy is safer. A closing question: will future derived contracts need to extend this feature, or should you lock it behind private to reduce risk?

keyIdea.title: Encapsulation vs reuse
keyIdea.text: Use private to strictly hide helpers; use internal to enable safe reuse by derived contracts while keeping functions inaccessible externally.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Private vs Internal
Inheritance hierarchy
Design members that should be shared with children as internal. Keep sensitive helpers private to prevent accidental overriding or misuse.
Private example
function _decrementCounterPrivate() private {
  _internalCounter--;
}
Internal example
function _getInternalCounter() internal view returns (uint) {
  return _internalCounter;
}
Checklist
  • Will derived contracts extend this behavior?
  • Could external callers misuse this helper?
  • Prefer internal for reusable logic, private for locked details.

screens.title: State mutability: view and pure
screens.narratorSegment: State mutability modifiers communicate whether a function may read or modify contract state. view functions promise not to modify state, though they may read storage variables. That promise allows clients to call them off-chain without creating a transaction, which costs no gas. However, if a view function is called within a transaction that changes state, it still consumes gas as part of that transaction. pure functions are stricter: they promise not to read or modify state. They operate only on input parameters and local variables. Pure functions are ideal for mathematics or deterministic transformations, like adding two numbers. For example, calculateSum declared pure will never touch storage, so it can be evaluated by a node or UI freely. A common pitfall is marking a function view when it accidentally modifies a state variable via an assignment; the compiler will catch many cases, but design discipline helps. Use view and pure to document intent for readers and tooling, and to reduce unnecessary gas when consumers use off-chain calls. Consider whether a function genuinely needs storage access; if not, mark it pure to be explicit.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › view and pure
view
Reads state but does not modify it. Free when called off-chain.
function getCurrentCounter() public view returns (uint) {
  return _internalCounter;
}
pure
Does not read or write state. Deterministic computation only.
function calculateSum(uint a, uint b) public pure returns (uint) {
  return a + b;
}
Key Takeaway

Choose view or pure to convey intent and enable gas-free reads from user interfaces and scripts.

screens.title: Payable functions and msg.value
screens.narratorSegment: A payable function explicitly allows the contract to receive Ether. By default, non-payable functions revert when Ether is sent, so marking a function payable is an explicit consent to accept funds. When a transaction calls a payable function, the amount of Wei sent is available as msg. value. Use msg. value to enforce minimum payments, update state, or record deposits. For instance, a register function can be payable and require msg. value to be at least a threshold such as 0.01 Ether; once checked, it can mark msg. sender in a mapping of registeredUsers and emit an event. When designing payable functions, check for reentrancy or unexpected state changes; plan whether funds are stored in the contract balance or forwarded immediately. A common withdrawal pattern is restricting withdraw functions by onlyOwner, checking the contract balance, and using an external call to transfer funds while checking the call success. Remember: payable is a safety feature. If you forget it on a function that should accept Ether, callers will find their transactions revert, which can be frustrating and costly. Always validate msg. value and emit events for auditability.

keyIdea.title: Payable rule
keyIdea.text: Mark functions payable to accept Ether; use msg.value to inspect the amount and enforce payment rules, then handle funds explicitly.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Payable functions
Example: register payable
function register() public payable {
  require(msg.value >= 0.01 ether, "Minimum fee required");
  registeredUsers[msg.sender] = true;
  emit Registered(msg.sender);
}
This function enforces a minimum payment, marks the sender as registered, and emits an event for auditing.
Withdraw pattern
function withdrawAll() public onlyOwner {
  require(address(this).balance > 0, "No Ether to withdraw.");
  (bool success, ) = owner.call{value: address(this).balance}("");
  require(success, "Withdrawal failed.");
}
Withdraw only when needed and check call success. Restrict to owner with a modifier to prevent misuse.

screens.title: Custom modifiers for reusable access control
screens.narratorSegment: Custom modifiers let you encapsulate reusable checks and inject them before a function runs. A modifier is declared with the modifier keyword and contains a placeholder underscore that indicates where the target function's code will execute. For access control, an onlyOwner modifier checks that msg. sender equals owner and reverts otherwise. Applied to functions, the modifier prevents unauthorized calls without duplicating the check in every function. Modifiers can also be used for input validation, rate limiting, or preconditions like ensuring a mapping entry exists. For example, onlyRegistered would check a registeredUsers mapping and revert when the caller is not registered. This both improves clarity and reduces the risk of missing a check. When writing modifiers, keep them fast and predictable; avoid complex logic that might hide side effects. Also, remember that modifiers are part of the function's execution flow: if a modifier reverts, the function body is never executed. Use events to surface modifier failures when appropriate. Finally, think about stacking modifiers to combine checks, but be mindful of gas cost and readability when multiple checks are applied. Custom modifiers for reusable access control means modifiers encapsulate reusable checks; they keep access control and validation centralized and reduce duplication across functions.. In practical terms, define modifiers like onlyowner and onlyregistered to centralize checks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Custom modifiers
onlyOwner example
modifier onlyOwner() {
  require(msg.sender == owner, "Only owner can call this function.");
  _;
}
Attach this modifier to functions to enforce owner-only execution without repeating the check.
onlyRegistered example
modifier onlyRegistered() {
  require(registeredUsers[msg.sender], "Not registered.");
  _;
}
Use this to gate access to view or action functions for registered users only.
Common mistake

Putting heavy logic in modifiers can hide side effects. Keep modifiers short and clear.

screens.title: Example contract: FunctionVisibilityAndModifiers
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a compact contract that brings together the concepts we have discussed. The contract declares an owner state variable and private and internal counters to demonstrate differing visibility on state. A custom onlyOwner modifier checks msg. sender against owner and inserts the guarded function code at the placeholder. The constructor sets owner to msg. sender and initializes state. Public functions like incrementCounterPublic are guarded by onlyOwner to restrict changes. Private helpers such as _decrementCounterPrivate are usable only within the same contract and cannot be called by derived contracts, enforcing strict encapsulation. Internal getters like _getInternalCounter can be reused by derived contracts. We see external functions like getOwner declared external view to emphasize external-only access and optimize calldata usage. The deposit function is payable and emits an event with msg. value and the updated contract balance. The withdrawAll function shows an owner-only withdrawal pattern with safety checks on balance and a call that returns success. This contract is a practical illustration: use visibility to limit access, mutability to document intent, payable to accept funds, and modifiers to centralize checks. keyIdea.title: Integrated example
keyIdea.text: A single contract can combine visibility, mutability, payable, and modifiers to express secure and readable behavior patterns.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Example contract
Key Solidity snippet
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract FunctionVisibilityAndModifiers {
  address public owner;
  uint private _internalCounter;
  uint internal _sharedData;

  modifier onlyOwner() {
    require(msg.sender == owner, "Only owner can call this function.");
    _;
  }

  constructor() {
    owner = msg.sender;
    _internalCounter = 0;
    _sharedData = 100;
  }

  function incrementCounterPublic() public onlyOwner {
    _internalCounter++;
  }

  function _decrementCounterPrivate() private {
    _internalCounter--;
  }

  function _getInternalCounter() internal view returns (uint) {
    return _internalCounter;
  }

  function getOwner() external view returns (address) {
    return owner;
  }

  function getCurrentCounter() public view returns (uint) {
    return _internalCounter;
  }

  function calculateSum(uint a, uint b) public pure returns (uint) {
    return a + b;
  }

  function deposit() public payable {
    emit DepositReceived(msg.sender, msg.value, address(this).balance);
  }

  function withdrawAll() public onlyOwner {

screens.title: Derived contracts and access to internal members
screens.narratorSegment: Derived contracts inherit state and behavior from a base contract and can call internal functions and read internal variables defined in their parent. In the example provided, DerivedContract extends FunctionVisibilityAndModifiers and accesses _sharedData and _getInternalCounter directly because both are internal. This pattern supports modular design: a base contract can offer internal utilities while derived contracts implement specialized behavior. Note that private members remain inaccessible to children; trying to call a private helper from a derived contract will cause a compilation error. Use internal when the design anticipates extending feature sets or when you want to expose controlled internals to plug-in modules. A practical guideline is to keep base contract internals stable and well-documented, since changes can break derived contracts. Additionally, be mindful of visibility for variables: public variables generate getter functions that are externally callable; internal variables do not expose automatic getters. When testing, add unit tests from the derived contract perspective to confirm access patterns. As a final reflection, ask whether the intended extension points are intentionally internal and minimal to avoid leaking implementation details to external callers. screens.title: Common pitfalls and misconceptions
screens.narratorSegment: Several recurrent mistakes can cause bugs or security issues. First, forgetting to mark functions payable if they must accept Ether leads to reverted transactions and poor user experience. Always confirm payable is present when your A P I accepts funds. Second, making helper functions public expands attack surface and may expose internal logic unintentionally; prefer private or internal for helpers. Third, confusing view and pure with gas: view and pure can be called off-chain for free, but if a view function is executed inside a transaction that modifies state, it still consumes gas as part of that transaction. Fourth, incorrectly attempting to call external functions internally as if they were public is a misuse; external functions read calldata directly and are not designed for internal direct calls. Fifth, placing heavy computation or external calls in modifiers can obscure control flow and make reasoning about gas harder. Finally, using call for transfers without checking success can lose funds silently; always test the withdraw pattern and assert success. The best defense is to write small functions, prefer internalized helpers, and include unit tests that cover edge cases like insufficient payments, unauthorized callers, and inheritance behavior.

screens.title: Quick design checklist
screens.narratorSegment: When designing a new function, follow a small checklist. First, ask whether this function needs to be callable from outside the contract. If not, prefer internal or private. Second, determine whether the function reads or writes state. If it only reads, mark it view; if it neither reads nor writes, mark it pure. Third, consider whether the function must accept Ether. If so, mark it payable and validate msg. value inside the function. Fourth, decide if there are common preconditions like ownership or registration; if so, create a modifier to centralize the check and apply it to every affected function. Fifth, consider gas: for large array inputs, external with calldata can be more efficient than public with memory copies. Finally, add events for state changes and payments for observability. Use this checklist as a short design loop when creating or reviewing functions. As a closing thought, run through one of your existing functions and ask whether it still meets these criteria or could be simplified. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn how to write functions that control behavior, security, and gas use in a Solidity contract. Functions are the executable units that accept inputs, optionally change state, return values, and enforce rules. We will look closely at visibility modifiers — public, private, internal and external — and why choosing the right one prevents accidental access and enforces encapsulation. You'll learn state mutability modifiers, view and pure, which help you signal read-only intent and reduce gas when called off-chain. We'll also show how payable marks a function able to accept Ether and how msg. value reports the amount sent. Finally, you'll meet custom modifiers, a compact pattern to reuse access checks like an onlyOwner guard. A concrete code example in this chapter demonstrates these ideas working together: constructor initialization, a payable deposit, an owner-only withdraw, internal helper functions, and a derived contract that can access internal members. Knowing these tools matters because they reduce bugs, tighten access control, and optimize costs. As you explore, ask yourself whether a function truly needs external exposure or can be internalized for safety.

By the end of these first objective cards you'll be able to define functions with appropriate parameters and return types, and understand how function signatures determine callable behavior. You will learn to select correct visibility modifiers — public, private, internal, and external — and to explain why each limits or permits calls in different contexts. We'll practice using view and pure to mark read-only behavior or pure computation so you can save gas on off-chain calls. Finally, you will begin to recognize when a function must be payable to accept Ether and how msg. value and the contract balance relate. Each objective is concrete: for example, you'll write a function signature that returns a uint and mark it view when it only reads storage. You'll write a payable register function that requires a minimum fee and updates a mapping. These skills matter because they reduce attack surface, make intent explicit, and help you design gas-efficient APIs. As you study, reflect on one question: which of your contract functions truly need external visibility and which can be internalized for safety?

This second objectives slide focuses on applying the concepts in design and tests. You'll practice deciding which functions should be external APIs and which should be internal helpers, and you'll implement simple modifiers to centralize checks like owner-only access or registration validation. The hands-on activity in this chapter asks you to build a token gating contract: a payable register function requires a minimum fee, adds the sender to a mapping, and a view function returns a welcome string only to registered users. You will also implement a withdraw function that only the owner can call. These exercises let you experience common pitfalls: forgetting payable, or making a helper public by accident. By designing and testing these patterns, you gain a practical sense of how visibility and mutability affect contract interfaces, gas costs, and security. After practicing, ask yourself whether your public A P I could be simplified by moving helpers internal or private to reduce risk.

A function in Solidity is a named, executable block that accepts parameters, optionally changes contract state, and may return values. The function signature—its name plus parameter types and return types—forms the contract's callable A P I. Signatures matter because the Ethereum ABI uses them to encode and decode calls, and because clarity in signature design reduces programmer error. For example, a function declared as returns (uint) signals to callers that they will receive a numeric result; marking it view communicates that the call will not alter state. A well-designed function is small, focused, and documents whether it reads or writes state. Common mistakes include over-exposing helpers as public, which expands attack surface, and neglecting to declare return types, which can confuse callers and tools. A concrete example: a function calculateSum(uint a, uint b) declared pure returns (uint) performs only a computation and does not access storage, so it is safe to call off-chain and is gas-free when executed via a read-only provider. Remember: signatures express intent and constraints; use them deliberately to make your contract predictable, testable, and secure. Which of your functions could be simplified to pure or view to clarify intent and reduce costs?

Visibility controls who can call a function and is a central part of contract design. Public functions are the most permissive: they can be called from external accounts or other contracts and also from inside the same contract. Because public is the default, explicitly declaring visibility improves readability. Private functions, by contrast, can only be called from within the defining contract; they cannot be accessed by derived contracts or external callers. Use private for helper logic that must never be shared. Internal functions sit between private and public: they are inaccessible externally but can be called by derived contracts. This makes internal suitable for shared logic in an inheritance hierarchy. External functions can only be called from outside the contract. They read arguments from calldata directly, which can be more gas-efficient for large arrays or strings compared to public functions that copy arguments into memory. A typical pattern is to expose an external function as the public A P I that validates inputs and then delegate to an internal function for the shared implementation, reducing duplication and protecting helpers. A common misconception is thinking external can be called internally like a normal function; it cannot. When designing visibility, ask: who should be allowed to call this, and could making it internal or private reduce risk?

Private and internal control how logic is shared across inheritance boundaries. Private restricts access strictly to the same contract body. Use it for helper functions or operations that must never be visible to children—for example, a low-level decrement helper that should only be used internally to avoid misuse. Internal, however, opens the function to derived contracts, enabling reuse inside an inheritance hierarchy without exposing it to external callers. This is often the right choice when you want to let child contracts extend behavior or read shared state variables like _sharedData in our example contract. A common pattern is to implement core behavior in internal functions and leave thin public or external wrappers for validation or input parsing. Misconceptions to avoid: internal is not public; it still cannot be called from external accounts. Another subtle point: state variables marked internal are accessible in derived contracts, but private variables are not. When designing inheritance, decide if children should have controlled access to your internals or if stricter privacy is safer. A closing question: will future derived contracts need to extend this feature, or should you lock it behind private to reduce risk?

State mutability modifiers communicate whether a function may read or modify contract state. view functions promise not to modify state, though they may read storage variables. That promise allows clients to call them off-chain without creating a transaction, which costs no gas. However, if a view function is called within a transaction that changes state, it still consumes gas as part of that transaction. pure functions are stricter: they promise not to read or modify state. They operate only on input parameters and local variables. Pure functions are ideal for mathematics or deterministic transformations, like adding two numbers. For example, calculateSum declared pure will never touch storage, so it can be evaluated by a node or UI freely. A common pitfall is marking a function view when it accidentally modifies a state variable via an assignment; the compiler will catch many cases, but design discipline helps. Use view and pure to document intent for readers and tooling, and to reduce unnecessary gas when consumers use off-chain calls. Consider whether a function genuinely needs storage access; if not, mark it pure to be explicit.

A payable function explicitly allows the contract to receive Ether. By default, non-payable functions revert when Ether is sent, so marking a function payable is an explicit consent to accept funds. When a transaction calls a payable function, the amount of Wei sent is available as msg. value. Use msg. value to enforce minimum payments, update state, or record deposits. For instance, a register function can be payable and require msg. value to be at least a threshold such as 0.01 Ether; once checked, it can mark msg. sender in a mapping of registeredUsers and emit an event. When designing payable functions, check for reentrancy or unexpected state changes; plan whether funds are stored in the contract balance or forwarded immediately. A common withdrawal pattern is restricting withdraw functions by onlyOwner, checking the contract balance, and using an external call to transfer funds while checking the call success. Remember: payable is a safety feature. If you forget it on a function that should accept Ether, callers will find their transactions revert, which can be frustrating and costly. Always validate msg. value and emit events for auditability.

Custom modifiers let you encapsulate reusable checks and inject them before a function runs. A modifier is declared with the modifier keyword and contains a placeholder underscore that indicates where the target function's code will execute. For access control, an onlyOwner modifier checks that msg. sender equals owner and reverts otherwise. Applied to functions, the modifier prevents unauthorized calls without duplicating the check in every function. Modifiers can also be used for input validation, rate limiting, or preconditions like ensuring a mapping entry exists. For example, onlyRegistered would check a registeredUsers mapping and revert when the caller is not registered. This both improves clarity and reduces the risk of missing a check. When writing modifiers, keep them fast and predictable; avoid complex logic that might hide side effects. Also, remember that modifiers are part of the function's execution flow: if a modifier reverts, the function body is never executed. Use events to surface modifier failures when appropriate. Finally, think about stacking modifiers to combine checks, but be mindful of gas cost and readability when multiple checks are applied. Custom modifiers for reusable access control means modifiers encapsulate reusable checks; they keep access control and validation centralized and reduce duplication across functions.. In practical terms, define modifiers like onlyowner and onlyregistered to centralize checks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through a compact contract that brings together the concepts we have discussed. The contract declares an owner state variable and private and internal counters to demonstrate differing visibility on state. A custom onlyOwner modifier checks msg. sender against owner and inserts the guarded function code at the placeholder. The constructor sets owner to msg. sender and initializes state. Public functions like incrementCounterPublic are guarded by onlyOwner to restrict changes. Private helpers such as _decrementCounterPrivate are usable only within the same contract and cannot be called by derived contracts, enforcing strict encapsulation. Internal getters like _getInternalCounter can be reused by derived contracts. We see external functions like getOwner declared external view to emphasize external-only access and optimize calldata usage. The deposit function is payable and emits an event with msg. value and the updated contract balance. The withdrawAll function shows an owner-only withdrawal pattern with safety checks on balance and a call that returns success. This contract is a practical illustration: use visibility to limit access, mutability to document intent, payable to accept funds, and modifiers to centralize checks. As a check: can you find which functions a derived contract may call and which it cannot?

Derived contracts inherit state and behavior from a base contract and can call internal functions and read internal variables defined in their parent. In the example provided, DerivedContract extends FunctionVisibilityAndModifiers and accesses _sharedData and _getInternalCounter directly because both are internal. This pattern supports modular design: a base contract can offer internal utilities while derived contracts implement specialized behavior. Note that private members remain inaccessible to children; trying to call a private helper from a derived contract will cause a compilation error. Use internal when the design anticipates extending feature sets or when you want to expose controlled internals to plug-in modules. Several recurrent mistakes can cause bugs or security issues. First, forgetting to mark functions payable if they must accept Ether leads to reverted transactions and poor user experience. Always confirm payable is present when your A P I accepts funds. Second, making helper functions public expands attack surface and may expose internal logic unintentionally; prefer private or internal for helpers. Third, confusing view and pure with gas: view and pure can be called off-chain for free, but if a view function is executed inside a transaction that modifies state, it still consumes gas as part of that transaction. Fourth, incorrectly attempting to call external functions internally as if they were public is a misuse; external functions read calldata directly and are not designed for internal direct calls. Fifth, placing heavy computation or external calls in modifiers can obscure control flow and make reasoning about gas harder. Finally, using call for transfers without checking success can lose funds silently; always test the withdraw pattern and assert success. The best defense is to write small functions, prefer internalized helpers, and include unit tests that cover edge cases like insufficient payments, unauthorized callers, and inheritance behavior.

When designing a new function, follow a small checklist. First, ask whether this function needs to be callable from outside the contract. If not, prefer internal or private. Second, determine whether the function reads or writes state. If it only reads, mark it view; if it neither reads nor writes, mark it pure. Third, consider whether the function must accept Ether. If so, mark it payable and validate msg. value inside the function. Fourth, decide if there are common preconditions like ownership or registration; if so, create a modifier to centralize the check and apply it to every affected function. Fifth, consider gas: for large array inputs, external with calldata can be more efficient than public with memory copies. Finally, add events for state changes and payments for observability. Use this checklist as a short design loop when creating or reviewing functions. These three cards collect the most important terms to remember. First, function signature: it is the name plus parameter and return types and defines the contract's callable A P I. Second, visibility modifiers: public allows external and internal calls, private restricts to the same contract, internal allows access by derived contracts, and external is callable only from outside and can be more gas-efficient for large calldata inputs. Third, state mutability: view reads state without modifying it and pure neither reads nor modifies state; both enable gas-free off-chain calls. Keep these succinct definitions in mind while you code, and use them to audit each function's declaration and intended use.
